slides.title: S.A.F.E.: Purpose, Scope, and Assurance
slides.transcript: Welcome to OCP S.A.F.E.: Product Security Reviews and S.O.L.I.D. Requirements. A device can have a familiar name and still contain firmware that changes its security behavior. This course helps you ask what was reviewed, what the evidence establishes, and how that evidence supports your own decisions.
slides.subtitle: Explain what a S.A.F.E. review establishes and match review depth to the threat model.

slides.title: From Product Risk to Review Evidence
slides.transcript: We'll follow three connected decisions. First, understand what an independent S.A.F.E. review covers and how the three review scopes relate to a threat model. Then prepare an engagement and learn how findings become useful evidence. Finally, connect S.O.L.I.D. product requirements and AI-assisted analysis to the review process. The course includes a program overview recording and six short questions. You don't need prior knowledge of either program.
modules_listed: Preparing, Completing, and Using a Review

slides.title: Firmware Is Part of the Trust Boundary
slides.transcript:
Firmware is software that controls a device's behavior close to the hardware. A storage controller, network adapter, or accelerator can depend on firmware to start securely, protect configuration, handle commands, and apply updates. The operating system isn't the only place where a security problem can matter.

Think about a storage device that accepts a firmware update. You need confidence in the code, where it came from, and the mechanism that decides whether the update is authorized. You also need to understand what happens to sensitive data and keys during normal operation, recovery, and changes of ownership.

These questions cross a trust boundary: a point where privileges or security assumptions change. A useful assessment connects the device's code and architecture to the assets it must protect. That gives you a reason to examine implementation evidence, rather than relying only on a product description.

bullets.text: Firmware controls security-relevant device behavior.
Updates, configuration, and secrets cross trust boundaries.
Assess code and architecture against the assets at risk.

slides.title: One Independent Review Can Serve Several Customers
slides.transcript:
Start with a vendor preparing a device for several customers. If each customer commissions an unrelated assessment, the vendor can face repeated requests for similar evidence and repeated review effort.

OCP S.A.F.E. means Security Appraisal Framework and Enablement. The vendor works with an approved independent Security Review Provider, or SRP, to assess the agreed product and firmware scope.

The review produces a bounded set of evidence. It identifies what was examined, the reviewed firmware, the scope, and the findings and limitations relevant to interpreting the result.

That evidence can then be shared with several customers. They can each evaluate the same review instead of beginning with an entirely separate assessment of the same material.

Each customer still checks the boundary. Does the product and firmware match? Does the review address the intended deployment and its risks? Reusable evidence reduces duplicate effort while leaving the customer's deployment decision with the customer.

slides.title: Three Scopes Follow the Threat Model
slides.transcript:
A threat model describes the assets to protect, the adversaries and their capabilities, and the ways those adversaries might reach the system. The review scope should follow those concerns.

Scope one is a code and architecture assessment. It includes white-box examination of firmware and its security-sensitive behavior, informed by the device's design and threat model. Examples include secure boot, handling of secrets, input validation, and privileged interfaces.

Scope two includes those areas and looks more deeply at trust boundaries. Think about isolation between application processing and a security processor, or the protections used when data and control cross those boundaries.

Scope three adds resilience to physical attacks. Fault injection and side-channel resistance become important when an attacker can interact physically with security-critical components.

These aren't three pass grades. They describe increasing assessment depth for the threat model. A device can have different components assessed at different depths. The provider and vendor agree the boundary and the applicable work, rather than assigning one universal depth to every part.

cards.title: Scope 1
cards.body: Code and architecture assessment: firmware, security-sensitive behavior, and implementation.

cards.title: Scope 2
cards.body: Includes Scope 1 and adds deeper focus on trust boundaries and isolation.

cards.title: Scope 3
cards.body: Includes lower-scope areas and adds resilience to physical attacks.

slides.subtitle: Select depth for the threat model; different components may need different depths.

slides.title: Choose Depth for the Asset at Risk
slides.transcript:
Consider three examples. A firmware command parser receives input from a less trusted source. You want the review to examine how that input is validated and whether it can corrupt memory or bypass authorization. That's a code and architecture concern associated with Scope one.

Now consider a system that separates application processing from a security function. The question is whether that separation really protects privileged operations and sensitive assets. A deeper trust-boundary assessment brings the emphasis of Scope two into view.

Finally, consider a long-lived device secret used by a hardware trust anchor. If an attacker can manipulate the device physically, the review may need to examine fault injection or information leakage through side channels. That's the additional emphasis of Scope three.

The examples show how to ask for the right depth. They don't replace the threat model or the provider's scoping judgment. Start with the asset and the attacker's capabilities, then agree the assessment needed.

Security boundary: isolation and protected operations.
Long-lived secret: fault injection and side-channel resistance.

slides.title: Read the Boundary Before Reusing a Result
slides.transcript:
A review result has a boundary. The product identity, firmware version or hash, assessed components, and review scope tell you what the evidence is about. Limitations and findings tell you where interpretation needs care.

Before reusing a result, compare that boundary with what you plan to deploy. A product family name alone doesn't establish that a different firmware build or configuration was examined. A later update may need a follow-up assessment, with the changes and baseline agreed by the vendor and provider.

Also consider the deployment. A remaining issue may have different consequences in different environments, and a documented mitigation still needs to be appropriate and implemented. S.A.F.E. supports an informed security decision. It doesn't guarantee that every version is vulnerability-free or that every deployment has the same risk.

bullets.text: Match product identity and firmware version or hash.
Check assessed components, scope, and limitations.
Evaluate remaining findings for the intended deployment.

slides.title: See the Review Process in Context
slides.transcript: Welcome to the OCP S.A.F.E. or S.A.F.E. program. In this course, you'll gain a foundational understanding of how the S.A.F.E. framework improves device security, streamlines audits, and supports supply chain assurance across modern data centers. Today's data centers use a diverse set of devices, CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, NICs, and storage systems, all of which run firmware or microcode that may be updated over time. These components form part of a complex software supply chain. Assuring the security and integrity of those devices is essential, especially as regulatory expectations increase globally. Historically, each customer or hyperscaler would request their own audit of a device, creating a patchwork of duplicated work and inconsistent reviews. This model led to delays, inefficiencies, and late discovery of vulnerabilities often during production or deployment. OCP S.A.F.E. was developed to address this problem. It allows a single structured review to serve multiple customers. The goal is simple, reduce audit overhead, share trustworthy results, and enable faster time to market while strengthening the overall security posture of device firmware. S.A.F.E. assessments are conducted by approved security review providers or SRPs. These are trusted third-party firms selected for their independence and technical depth. Each engagement starts with a scope definition. The device vendor and the SRP align on which scopes will be in scope and within each scope which sections apply to the device under test. As part of this early phase, the device vendor is expected to socialize the scope definition with their cloud service provider. Scope 1 addresses privileged firmware and software on a single device. It includes design review, threat modeling, code analysis, and code review. Scope 2 examines architectural isolation of critical components, like management co-processors or TEEs. It relies on hardware design and code reviews, not live attacks. Scope 3 focuses on resilience to physical attacks and the protection of long-term secrets. It includes an analysis of SoC design and fault injection protections. S.A.F.E. reviews are document-driven. The SRP examines firmware, HDL, design documentation, and threat models using white box methods rather than reverse engineering. Device vendors submit artifacts including source code, firmware binaries, and any relevant security models. The SRP reviews and identifies any weaknesses. The review is collaborative. Vendors address findings and resubmit until the assessment meets the safe criteria. The SRP produces two deliverables. The first is a detailed report for the vendor's internal use. The second is a concise, signed summary known as the short-form report. The device vendor can choose to embargo a short-form report where there is concern about publicly disclosing certain findings. This short-form report includes the firmware hash, review scope, SRP name, and whether any vulnerabilities were found. Short-form reports are submitted to OCP's GitHub repository and optionally listed in the OCP marketplace. Consumers can verify audit status without repeating the review. S.A.F.E. ensures that firmware security reviews happen early and can be reused across vendors and cloud platforms. This supports consistent assurance and scalable compliance. The short-form supports reference integrity manifests or RIMs, which help match measured device values to the firmware that was reviewed. S.A.F.E. does not replace regulatory programs like FIPS. It complements them by focusing specifically on firmware level review outcomes and transparency. Several companies have already participated, AMD submitted a GPU, SK hynix reviewed an SSD, and Intel demonstrated end-to-end attestation. As the program evolves, more SRPs and device types will be supported. S.A.F.E. is designed to be flexible, accommodating a range of architectures, use cases, and threat models. In this course will guide you through how to prepare for a safe review, define scope, engage with an SRP, and submit results. S.A.F.E. reflects a shift towards shared security responsibility. It builds trust between producers and consumers, and reduces time to assurance across the ecosystem.

slides.title: Scope and Evidence Guide the Decision
slides.transcript: Keep four ideas together. S.A.F.E. provides independent review evidence. Sharing that evidence can reduce duplicate assessment effort. The three scopes connect review depth to the threat model. And a result must be read within its product, firmware, and assessment boundary. When you encounter a review report, ask what it actually covers before deciding how to use it.
items: Scopes describe review focus, not pass grades.
Check product, firmware, scope, and limitations.

slides.title: Preparing, Completing, and Using a Review
slides.transcript: A useful independent review begins with a clear question about a real product. This module follows the vendor and review provider from preparation through analysis, remediation, and reporting, so you can recognize the evidence a customer will need.
slides.subtitle: Prepare a useful review brief and distinguish private findings, public evidence, and customer decisions.

slides.title: Build a Review Brief That Others Can Use
slides.transcript: By the end of this module, you'll be able to define the assessment boundary, prepare a practical evidence and access brief, and explain how the vendor and Security Review Provider turn findings into review deliverables. You'll also distinguish the private technical report from the public short-form report and recognize when changed firmware needs further attention.
objectives: Separate the assessment boundary from review depth.
Prepare technical evidence, access, and confidentiality arrangements.
Explain remediation, verification, and reporting responsibilities.

slides.title: Define What Is Being Assessed
slides.transcript:
Two scoping decisions are easy to confuse. The first is what you're asking the provider to assess. That might be a complete device, a particular component, or a change relative to an earlier reviewed baseline. The second is the depth of review, expressed through Scopes one, two, and three.

A component review isn't automatically a Scope one review. A small security component can require physical-attack analysis, while a larger system can contain several areas with different assessment needs.

For a firmware update, a differential review focuses attention on the changes and their implications. The provider needs an agreed baseline and enough information to understand what changed, including relevant dependencies and interactions. It isn't a promise that every update will be a small or inexpensive assessment.

Prepare a brief that separates the product boundary from the requested depth. Then discuss both with the approved provider and the customers who will depend on the result.

bullets.text: Boundary: whole device, component, or agreed changes.
Depth: the applicable numbered review scopes.
Differential review: establish the baseline and implications of change.

figure.caption: The assessment boundary and the review depth are separate decisions.
figure.alt: The assessment boundary and the review depth are separate decisions.

slides.title: Prepare the Evidence and the Access
slides.transcript:
Start with the product's purpose and intended use. Give the provider a clear architecture description, the relevant components, and the assets and interfaces that matter to security. A threat model helps connect those details to realistic adversaries and attack surfaces.

Prepare the source code, firmware information, and build material needed for white-box review. Explain third-party dependencies and supply a software bill of materials, often called an SBOM. The provider can then understand which components are present and how inherited issues may affect the product.

Access and confidentiality need practical arrangements too. Agree how the provider will inspect the material, which environment will be used, and the appropriate engagement and confidentiality terms. If a threat model is missing, discuss how it will be developed as part of the work.

Use OCP's maintained list of approved providers. The goal is a provider with the technical capability and access needed for this product, supported by a preparation set that makes the assessment possible.

bullets.text: Product purpose, architecture, interfaces, and threat model.
Source, firmware, build information, and dependencies.
Software bill of materials and appropriate secure access.
Engagement and confidentiality arrangements with an approved provider.

slides.title: Review, Fix, and Verify
slides.transcript:
First, agree the scope and the access needed to evaluate it. The vendor, provider, and relevant customers need a shared understanding of the product, firmware, and assessment boundary.

The independent provider then examines the architecture, code, and supporting evidence, and identifies findings within that scope.

The vendor addresses the findings. That can mean changing code, strengthening a design, establishing and documenting a secure supported configuration, or preparing other appropriate remediation.

The provider checks the changes and verifies the claimed fixes. Vendor action and independent verification are separate responsibilities.

Sometimes verification shows that more work is needed. The finding returns to the vendor, and the provider evaluates the revised response. This visible return is part of the review process.

The final evidence records the reviewed state, outcomes, limitations, and any remaining reportable findings. A final report doesn't mean every concern has disappeared.

Engaging during design can make this work more useful, because an architectural issue is easier to address before a device is committed to production.

slides.title: Understand the Three Evidence Artifacts
slides.transcript:
Three evidence artifacts answer different questions. The scope document explains the assessment boundary: what was included, the areas examined, and the agreed context. It helps you decide whether the work matches the question you're asking.

The detailed report gives the vendor the technical analysis. It can describe methodology, limitations, findings, their impact, and recommended remediation. This material is generally private and may be protected by confidentiality agreements.

The short-form report, or SFR, is the signed machine-readable summary used for publication. It identifies the vendor, device, and reviewed firmware, including a firmware hash, and records the required review results. Use the maintained specification for its exact format and reporting rules.

These artifacts complement each other. A signature helps establish the integrity and origin of a report; it doesn't expand the review scope. To interpret the assurance, connect the identified product and firmware to the scope and the reported outcomes.
rows: What was found, how, and with what limitations?
Private technical analysis for the vendor

slides.title: Publish Responsibly and Review Changes
slides.transcript:
Published S.A.F.E. evidence is available through the OCP program's repository. Approved products can be promoted and found through the OCP Marketplace. The Marketplace link on this slide opens the OCP S.A.F.E. listings. Use a listing to identify the product, then follow the published review evidence. Vendors can use the Solution Provider guidance to learn the listing requirements.

The current framework puts the publication submission with the Device Vendor. This gives the vendor control over the timing and messaging around disclosure. A vendor can delay publication or decline it, but then forgoes the associated S.A.F.E. endorsement.

Publication isn't the end of product security work. When firmware or relevant implementation details change, agree the follow-up assessment needed for the changed state. A change-focused review can avoid repeating irrelevant work, but its effort depends on the changes and the review boundary.

For a customer, the practical habit stays the same: identify the deployed state, find the applicable evidence, and evaluate the findings and limitations for the intended use.

slides.title: A Useful Review Has a Clear Boundary and Follow-through
slides.transcript: A review engagement becomes useful when its boundary, evidence, and responsibilities are clear. Define what is being assessed separately from the depth of review. Prepare the architecture, threat model, code and build access, and dependency information. Let the vendor address findings and the independent provider verify the response. Then read the scope, detailed analysis, and signed summary for the questions each can answer.
items: Agree boundary and depth as separate decisions.
Prepare evidence and access that make review possible.
Vendor remediation and provider verification have distinct roles.
Use scope, detailed analysis, and signed results together.

slides.transcript: Apply the preparation and scoping ideas in these two questions. First, consider what must be agreed for a change-focused firmware review. slides.title: S.O.L.I.D. Requirements and AI-Assisted Reviews
slides.transcript: How do you move from broad security review areas to the requirements for a particular product? This module introduces S.O.L.I.D. and explains how product requirements, vendor evidence, and AI-assisted analysis fit within the S.A.F.E. review process.
slides.subtitle: Explain how applicable S.O.L.I.D. requirements and AI-assisted analysis fit within an independent S.A.F.E. review.

slides.title: Connect Requirements, Evidence, and Review
slides.transcript: You'll learn to explain the relationship between S.O.L.I.D. and S.A.F.E., find the requirement groups that apply to a product, and connect a requirement to evidence. You'll also see how the independent provider uses AI analysis while retaining responsibility for the review.
objectives: Explain how S.O.L.I.D. requirements fit within S.A.F.E.
Find applicable groups and connect requirements to evidence.
Describe independent provider responsibility in AI-assisted review.

slides.title: S.O.L.I.D. Makes Product Requirements Concrete
slides.transcript:
S.O.L.I.D. stands for Securing Of Latest Infrastructure Devices. It defines baseline security requirements for products used in data centers and a structure for identifying which requirements apply to different product types.

Think of three connected parts. The product type and its characteristics determine the applicable requirements. The vendor explains how those requirements are met and prepares supporting evidence. The independent provider evaluates the product through the S.A.F.E. process and records the results and gaps.

This isn't a second, unrelated audit process. The requirements make the review question more concrete: what should this kind of product provide, and what evidence supports that claim? Start with the applicability mapping, then use the full published requirements. The course examples show how to navigate that relationship; they aren't complete compliance checklists.

slides.title: Start With the Product Type
slides.transcript:
Start with a storage drive and the published product-type mapping.

Common requirement groups apply across products. They include general security properties, business processes, software, firmware, and cryptography. The exact requirement text determines what must be supported.

Then consider applicable conditions. A physical product brings hardware requirements. A product with a CPU or a PCIe interface brings the corresponding requirement groups. Check the actual design rather than assuming every drive is identical.

The disk-specific additions include sanitization under requirement STRG002. For a self-encrypting drive, the mapping also includes STRG001, concerning standardized storage security functionality. Those additions sit alongside the common and conditional groups.

An accelerator has a different set of additions, including system memory and root-of-trust requirements. Platform requirements also apply if it isn't enclosed in a server. The comparison shows why product type matters. Use the full mapping and requirements for the real product, rather than treating this illustration as the entire requirement set.

slides.title: Turn a Requirement Into Evidence
slides.transcript:
Take the storage-drive sanitization requirement as a simple example. The published requirement refers to the governing sanitization guidance and the S.A.F.E. storage sanitization requirements. Begin with that complete text, not just a marketing statement that the drive can erase data.

The vendor explains how the applicable behavior is implemented and provides evidence the provider can evaluate. Preparation might include design information, supported commands and states, test results, and the limits or conditions of the claimed behavior. These are illustrative evidence examples, rather than a complete prescribed test method.

The independent provider assesses the evidence and implementation within the agreed scope, and records the results and any gaps. Keeping the requirement, the vendor's claim, and the reviewed evidence connected makes it easier for a customer to understand what was established and what still needs attention.

slides.title: AI Expands Analysis; the Provider Owns the Review
slides.transcript:
Regular review by a security expert remains part of the assessment. The provider uses judgment to understand the design, its threat model, and the significance of findings.

AI-assisted analysis adds another way to examine the code. The provider runs the AI tool through suitable orchestration, so the analysis can cover the intended material and stay focused on the review.

The provider then triages the findings. A tool's output needs validation and interpretation before it becomes a review result.

The vendor addresses the issues that need remediation and supplies the response and evidence.

The provider verifies the changes and remains responsible for the final report. The AI tool doesn't take ownership of the assurance decision.

A vendor's internal scans can improve preparation, but handing their output to the provider doesn't replace the provider running the independent AI review. The published guidance also describes suitable model access and terms that protect confidential material.

slides.title: Know Which Requirement Applies When
slides.transcript:
Keep two effective dates separate. Starting October first, twenty twenty-six, applicable S.O.L.I.D. gaps must be listed in the long-form report. The checked guidance identifies short-form gap listing as future work without an effective date.

The AI scanning rule applies to audits with a completion date on or after January first, twenty twenty-seven. Before that threshold, AI review is optional but strongly recommended. Expert review remains required. Consult the current program guidance when planning an engagement, because requirements and tool guidance can evolve.

slides.title: Use Requirements to Ask Better Questions
slides.transcript: S.O.L.I.D. makes product expectations concrete, and the applicability mapping tells you which requirement groups to examine. Vendor claims need supporting evidence, and S.A.F.E. provides the independent review process. AI analysis can expand the examination, while the provider retains responsibility for evaluating findings and reporting results. Use those connections to ask better questions about the product you intend to supply or deploy.
items: Find the applicable product requirement groups.
Use the independent S.A.F.E. review process.

A correct answer isn't required for course completion.
